1.pericope_label: Son of man, say unto the prince of Tyrus, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because thine heart is lifted up, and thou hast said, I am a God, I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the seas
debates: Who the prince of Tyre was
Whether he literally claimed divine honours
How the comparison with Daniel should be rendered
outliers: Clarke lists Hiram, the devil, Ithobaal and, from Origen, the guardian angel of the city, and prefers Ithobaal on chronological grounds; Gill names Ethbaal after Josephus, rejects the Hiram identification as a rabbinic fable, and takes the prince as an emblem of antichrist rather than of the devil

Henry holds he had the impudence to speak the claim out; Ellicott denies he actually claimed religious homage and reads the words as a proud sense of self-sufficiency only translated into speech by the text; Wesley puts the saying in the heart
Gill reports that the Septuagint, Syriac and Arabic versions render the clause interrogatively, asking whether he is not wiser than Daniel
Ellicott takes the seat of God locally, of Tyre as the holy island and the central sanctuary of its colonies, where Wesley reads it simply as impregnable as heaven
themes: A dirge said to allude frequently to the fall of Lucifer
A condition named the insanity of prosperity, with a list of kings who suffered it
A temple called the oldest sanctuary in the annals of mankind
Men eminently successful in other walks of life who have sacrificed to their own net

4.pericope_label: Behold, therefore I will bring strangers upon thee, the terrible of the nations: and they shall draw their swords against the beauty of thy wisdom, and they shall defile thy brightness
debates: Whether the terrible of the nations must mean the Chaldeans
How the clause about being a man should be rendered
What the deaths of the uncircumcised are
outliers: Gill and Clarke name the Chaldean army outright; Ellicott notes the phrase is used of them elsewhere but is by no means necessarily confined to them

Ellicott would drop the future supplied in italics, since the form matches the earlier verse exactly and should be translated the same way, bringing out the contrast between the weakness of man and the power of God

Gill, Clarke and Wesley read the deaths as two, temporal and eternal; Ellicott reads the term for its force rather than its number, as carrying the opprobrium a Jew attached to the uncircumcised and amounting to profane and impious
Ellicott holds the plural reproduces a rare form of the original and emphatically indicates a violent death
themes: A king who got all by himself and believed he could keep all by himself
Swords drawn against the beauty of wisdom, explained as a way of naming the city
A bitter sarcasm asking whether a man will assert his deity to the face of his killer
The prince to be figured as the first man, perfect in Eden until driven out

11.pericope_label: Son of man, take up a lamentation upon the king of Tyrus, and say unto him, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Thou sealest up the sum, full of wisdom, and perfect in beauty
debates: Whether the lamentation has a sense beyond the literal
How thou sealest up the sum should be rendered
What the word rendered pipes means
outliers: Henry reports an allegory of the fall of the angels but prefers to refer any mystical sense to the fall of Adam; Gill reports both readings without deciding and notes that passages are interpreted of Adam in the Talmud; Clarke takes the Eden comparison as strong irony
Henry reports a view that the king of Tyre means the whole royal family, reaching back to Hiram, and notes that the earlier title is prince while this one is king
Clarke endorses a rendering that makes it thou drawest thy own likeness; Ellicott takes it as marking something complete or perfect; Wesley reads it as the king fancying such fulness in himself
Ellicott holds the word rendered pipes occurs only here and probably means females who played upon tambourines, where Wesley hears the lute and tabret of a coronation
themes: A word for sum used elsewhere only of a well measured building
Stones matching the breastplate of the high priest with one row omitted, which the Greek supplies
A king whose ornaments stood ready at his accession as everything was made ready for Adam
A situation as pleasant as the garden, at least in his own imagination

14.pericope_label: Thou art the anointed cherub that covereth; and I have set thee so: thou wast upon the holy mountain of God; thou hast walked up and down in the midst of the stones of fire
debates: What the stones of fire are
Whether the tense should be present or past
outliers: Clarke takes the stones of fire for floors paved with sparkling stones and Wesley for stones sparkling about the king; Ellicott rejects that as making the expression strange and prefers the paved work of sapphire beneath the feet of God; Clarke reports a further view that they are the stars, on which the passage would refer to the fall of Satan
Gill and Ellicott refer the cherub to the pair over the mercy seat, Ellicott tracing the whole imagery to the temple on Mount Zion; Clarke offers as well the cherub that guarded the gate of Paradise
Ellicott corrects the tense, since the Hebrew does not express it and the simple past used throughout the passage should be supplied
Ellicott notices the language passing from the king to the state he presided over and identified himself with, then returning to him personally
themes: A Latin poet quoted for apartments of marble, onyx and ebony brought from Meroe
A king told that the God he forgets is the one who made him so
A man said to have been like the angels, like Moses, like Adam, like God, until his iniquity was found
A holy mountain read ironically of a city rising out of the sea

18.pericope_label: Son of man, set thy face against Zidon, and prophesy against it, And say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against thee, O Zidon; and I will be glorified in the midst of thee
debates: Why Zidon needed a separate word of prophecy
How the glorifying and the sanctifying are related
outliers: Gill offers the palaces of the king and nobles, following Kimchi, or the temples of their gods; Ellicott holds they are not so much the actual temples as the ideal holy mountain in which the prince was figured as a covering cherub, and reports that many Hebrew manuscripts have the singular

Ellicott says there are several obvious reasons besides making up the number of the nations to seven; Henry finds the reason in Zidon being more addicted to idolatry than Tyre, whose men of business were less under the power of superstition

Henry treats the two as one, since when God is sanctified he is glorified, his holiness being his glory; Keil and Delitzsch read the glorifying historically, as upon Pharaoh, and effected by the judgments themselves
Ellicott draws from the iniquity of the traffic the rule that sin consists in the abuse of the very blessings God had given and leads directly to its own punishment
themes: A king who must have had sanctuaries as God, as the angels, as the cherubim, and defiled them
An object of adoration becoming a subject of horror
A city burnt entirely by one conqueror as it had been before by another
Borderers who might have learned to glorify God and seduced his people instead

22.pericope_label: And say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against thee, O Zidon; and I will be glorified in the midst of thee: and they shall know that I am the LORD, when I shall have executed judgments in her
debates: When the gathering of Israel takes place
Whether the overthrow of Zidon is as complete as that of Tyre
What the brier and the thorn stand for
outliers: Gill denies the gathering is the return from Babylon, since the ten tribes did not then return, and places it in the latter day; Clarke keeps it historical, as the return prepared for by the judgments on the surrounding nations; Ellicott takes the immediate point to be the return but holds the promise of rest looks forward in some sense to a final victory over all evil

Ellicott notes that no such utter desolation is foretold of Zidon as of Tyre, and that nothing is said of her special sins and very little of her overthrow, these being already known or covered by what was said of Tyre

Clarke suspects an allusion to a particular marriage that brought idolatry into Israel; Wesley makes the metaphors stand for the troublesome neighbours generally, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Tyre and Zidon, and holds the promise not yet fully accomplished
themes: A mother city outgrown by its own colony
Judgment beginning at the house of God and proceeding to the nations
A land prepared during the captivity so that the return should be safe
Ways of God called all equal, partialities and caprices belonging not to him
